After school, the boys and girls of the kasba gathered at Bhola's tea stall by the bus stand, and Samir, as usual, did most of the talking.
"My chacha sent money from the Gulf again," he said, flashing a new phone. "Big amount. Next month, a bike."
Pooja, sitting on the bench with her geography notes, glanced at the others. One boy rolled his eyes. Another suddenly remembered he had to fetch milk.
"You should see our new fridge," Samir went on. "Double door. Nobody in this whole town has one."
Pooja closed her notebook. "We've heard about the fridge, Samir."
He laughed and kept going, now about his cousin's car. He didn't see the two girls from his class quietly pick up their bags and walk toward the temple road. By the time his tea was finished, only Pooja was left, and she was only waiting for her bus.

qa.a: He said his chacha sent money from the Gulf again.

qa.a: Pooja finds it tiring and repetitive, which is why she reminds him they've heard about the fridge and only stays for her bus.

Monday. Salma didn't get the team-lead role. At home she told herself, over and over: I'm useless at numbers. Everyone saw it. I should never have applied.
Thursday. Still heavy, she opened her notebook and wrote a question her old teacher used to ask: "What evidence would change my mind?" Under it she listed: the quarterly report she built alone, the error she caught in March, the two teammates who ask her for help with spreadsheets. She stared at the list. "Hm," she said aloud.
The next Tuesday, she asked Yusuf, who had been on the panel, for five minutes. "Be honest. Was it my numbers?"
Yusuf shook his head. "Your numbers are the best on the team. It was presenting. You rushed the slides."
Salma nodded slowly. Presenting, she could practise. The heavy feeling eased. She booked a speaking workshop that evening.

qa.q: What did Salma list as evidence in her notebook?
qa.a: The quarterly report she built alone, the error she caught in March, and the two teammates who ask her for help with spreadsheets.

qa.q: How did Salma feel on Monday after missing the role?
qa.a: Salma felt crushed and ashamed, harshly telling herself she was useless at numbers.

qa.q: What worked better than self-attack?
qa.a: Kind, steady questions about evidence and asking Yusuf for honest feedback, which showed the real issue was presenting, something she could practise.

qa.q: How might Yusuf feel when Salma asks him directly?
qa.a: Yusuf likely feels respected and glad to help, since he can give her a clear, useful answer.

grounding: It shows a young adult replacing harsh self-attack with gentle questions about evidence, and her story about herself changing over several days.

passage:
Indu, you think everyone at your office is against you? Sit. Your Ojas Mama believed the same thing once.
I was twenty-five, at my first design firm. I was sure the seniors laughed at my work. If two people whispered, it was about me. If my drawing was sent back, it proved it.
One evening, I told my friend Kannan all of this at the tea shop. He listened, and then asked, "Ojas, if I told you this same story about my office, what would you say to me?"
I opened my mouth. I would have said, "Kannan, are you sure? Have you asked them?" I laughed, because I had my answer.
The next week, I asked my senior why my drawing came back. She said, "The measurements are off. The idea is good." That was all. Nobody was laughing.
I didn't need to shout at myself. I needed a kind question.

qa.q: What did Ojas's senior say about the drawing?
qa.a: She said, "The measurements are off. The idea is good."

qa.q: How did young Ojas feel when he realised his own answer to Kannan's question?
qa.a: He felt relieved and a little foolish, laughing because he saw that he would never believe such a story from a friend.

qa.q: What turning point in the story helped Ojas test his belief?
qa.a: When Kannan asked what Ojas would say to a friend with the same story, and Ojas then asked his senior directly about the drawing.

qa.q: How might Kannan have felt listening to Ojas at the tea shop?
qa.a: Kannan was probably concerned but patient, choosing a gentle question instead of arguing.

grounding: An uncle recalls testing his belief that colleagues were against him by asking what he would tell a friend, and finding the evidence did not support it.

passage:
Pranav held the new crayon box with both hands in the stationery shop.
"Only if you share with Sabina," Mumma said.
"I promise! I promise, promise!" He meant every word.
At home, his little sister Sabina reached for the red crayon. Pranav pulled the box to his chest. "No! Mine!"
"But you promised," Mumma said softly.
Pranav's lip wobbled. In the shop, sharing had felt easy. Now the red crayon felt like everything.
Mumma sat beside him. "Promises are hard when the feeling changes, na? Let's give Sabina two colours to start."
Slowly, Pranav held out the blue and the green.

qa.q: Which crayon did Sabina reach for?
qa.a: Sabina reached for the red crayon.

qa.q: Why did Pranav's lip wobble?
qa.a: Pranav felt sad and torn, because he had meant his promise in the shop but now wanted to keep the red crayon.

qa.q: How did Mumma help Pranav keep his promise?
qa.a: She stayed gentle, named that promises are hard when feelings change, and suggested a small start of two colours.

qa.q: How does Sabina experience the moment Pranav shouts "Mine"?
qa.a: Sabina is probably surprised and upset, since she expected to share the new crayons.

grounding: It shows a young child promising to share with full sincerity and then struggling when his later self feels differently.

passage:
"Sumit, can you tidy the blocks after you play?"
"Yes, Papa! I promise!"
"And Abhinav, you'll help your brother?"
"I promise too!"
Later, blocks everywhere. Sumit lay on the sofa.
"Sumit, you promised."
"I'm tired, Papa."
"But you said you would."
"That was before. I wasn't tired before." Sumit's eyes filled with tears.
Abhinav picked up two blocks. "I promised too."
Papa knelt down. "When you promise, it's also for later-you. Tired Sumit has to do what happy Sumit said."
Sumit sniffed. "Can tired Sumit do only the red ones?"
Papa smiled. "Tired Sumit can start with the red ones."

qa.q: What did Sumit promise to do after playing?
qa.a: He promised to tidy the blocks.

qa.q: Why did Sumit's eyes fill with tears?
qa.a: Sumit felt tired and sad, and confused that the promise he meant earlier now felt too hard.

qa.q: How did Papa help Sumit understand promises?
qa.a: Papa explained kindly that a promise is also for "later-you" and let him start small with the red ones.

qa.q: What is it like for Abhinav when Sumit won't tidy?
qa.a: Abhinav wants to keep that promise too and feels a little proud picking up blocks, even when Sumit lies on the sofa.

grounding: It shows small children promising to tidy up and meaning it, then finding the later tired self feels differently.

passage:
Nursery class note to parents, Tuesday.
At the gate this morning, Swati hugged her Mumma and said very seriously, "I promise I won't cry today." She meant it fully.
When the gate closed, her face crumpled. "But I promised," she sobbed, and cried harder.
Sharmila, who sits next to her, came and held her hand without a word. I told Swati, "Missing Mumma is okay. Feelings can change even after we promise."
Soon she was playing at the sand tray with Sharmila. At home, you might promise something small together instead, like one big hug at the gate.

qa.q: What did Swati promise her Mumma at the gate?
qa.a: She said, "I promise I won't cry today."

qa.q: Why did Swati cry harder after saying "But I promised"?
qa.a: Swati felt sad and worried that she had broken her promise, on top of missing Mumma.

qa.q: What did the teacher suggest to the parents?
qa.a: The teacher suggested promising something small together at home, like one big hug at the gate.

qa.q: How might Sharmila have felt when she held Swati's hand?
qa.a: Sharmila probably felt caring and a little worried for her friend, so she offered comfort without words.

grounding: A nursery teacher notes a small child who fully meant her promise not to cry and was upset when her feelings changed later.

passage:
On Saturday morning, the school's football ground was nearly empty when Rajni arrived for the inter-school match, sweaty and out of breath.
She had promised Sahil on Monday that she would come watch his first match as goalkeeper. Then, on Friday, her best friend Meenu invited her to a birthday party with a magic show, at the same time. Rajni had spent all night wishing she could be in two places.
She stood by the fence. Her stomach felt heavy. Everyone at the party would be laughing right now.
Then Sahil saw her. He waved both gloves wildly. "You came!"
During the second half, he saved a penalty and turned to look at her, grinning.
On the way home, her mother asked, "Was it worth missing the magic show?"
Rajni thought about Sahil's face. "Yes. He knew I'd come."

qa.q: What did Sahil play as in his first match?
qa.a: He played as goalkeeper.

qa.q: How did Rajni feel standing by the fence?
qa.a: Rajni felt heavy and disappointed, still wishing she could be at the party with the magic show.

qa.q: What would you say to Rajni about her choice?
qa.a: Keeping her word even when it was inconvenient showed Sahil she is someone he can rely on.

qa.q: What was it like for Sahil when he saw Rajni by the fence?
qa.a: Sahil felt happy and supported, waving both gloves and looking to her after his penalty save.

grounding: It shows a schoolchild keeping a promise to come to a friend's match despite a more tempting invitation, building a sense of being reliable.

passage:
Monday. On the walk home, Mridul told Rekha a secret: he still slept with the light on because the dark scared him. "Promise you won't tell?" "Promise," Rekha said.
Wednesday. At lunch, the other kids were laughing about who was scared of what. "Mridul looks like someone who's scared of the dark," one boy joked. Everyone turned to Rekha, who knew Mridul best. The secret was right on her tongue, and she wanted to laugh with them. Her cheeks went hot. "No idea," she said, and took a big bite of her roti.
The next Monday, Mridul waited for her at the gate. "Rekha, can I tell you something else? I'm nervous about the swimming test."
Rekha felt something warm in her chest. He trusted her. And she knew, somehow, that she was the kind of person who kept things.

qa.q: What secret did Mridul tell Rekha on Monday?
qa.a: He still slept with the light on because the dark scared him.

qa.q: What was Rekha feeling when everyone turned to her at lunch?
qa.a: Rekha felt tempted and embarrassed, wanting to laugh with the group but uneasy about breaking her promise.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Saying "No idea" and keeping the secret worked, because Mridul's trust grew and he shared more with her.

qa.q: How does Mridul see Rekha the next Monday?
qa.a: Mridul sees her as someone safe to trust, so he tells her his worry about the swimming test.

grounding: It shows a child keeping a friend's harmless secret through temptation over several days, building reputation and an inner sense of reliability.

passage:
Trisha, you want to skip your friend's dance show because it's raining? Let your Sunaina Nani tell you about the rain of 1968.
I was ten. My friend Kamla had a small part in the temple play, just one line. I had promised to sit in the front row. That evening the sky opened. Mud everywhere. My mother said, "Stay home, she won't even notice."
I sat at the window, wanting to stay dry so badly. But I had said it. Promise. I took Father's big black umbrella and walked, my feet squelching in my chappals.
When I arrived, soaking, Kamla was peeping from behind the curtain, looking at the front row. When she saw me, she smiled so big she almost forgot her line.
After that, she always said, "Sunaina comes. Even in rain." I liked being that person. I still do.

qa.q: What did young Sunaina take to walk in the rain?
qa.a: She took Father's big black umbrella.

qa.q: How did young Sunaina feel at the window before leaving?
qa.a: She felt torn and reluctant, badly wanting to stay dry but uneasy about breaking her promise.

qa.q: At what turning point did Sunaina choose to keep her word?
qa.a: At the window, when she decided "I had said it. Promise," and walked out despite the mud.

qa.q: How did Kamla feel when she saw Sunaina in the front row?
qa.a: Kamla felt happy and relieved, smiling so big she almost forgot her line.

grounding: A grandmother recalls keeping a childhood promise through heavy rain and how it built her sense of being reliable.

passage:
The inter-school debate final was at four in the school auditorium in Lucknow. At breakfast, Ishita's father Ramesh had said, "I'll be there, front row. Promise." He had said the same about the science fair in August, and the prize day in November.
At 3:55, Ishita looked at the front row. Her mother was there, holding up her phone to record. The seat beside her was empty.
Ishita won second place. On stage, she smiled for the photo.
At night, Ramesh knocked on her door. "Beta, I'm so sorry. The client meeting ran over. Next time, definitely."
"It's fine, Papa," Ishita said, not looking up from her book. "I didn't expect you."
He stood there for a moment. That hurt him more than if she had shouted. And she realised, with a strange calm, that she had stopped asking him to come to anything.

qa.q: What place did Ishita win in the debate final?
qa.a: Ishita won second place.

qa.q: How did Ishita feel when she said "I didn't expect you"?
qa.a: Ishita felt disappointed and numb, having stopped hoping after many broken promises, which is why she spoke with a strange calm.

qa.q: What could Ramesh do to start rebuilding Ishita's trust?
qa.a: He could stop making big promises he cannot keep, choose one event, block that time, and show up.

qa.q: How does Ramesh feel when Ishita says she didn't expect him?
qa.a: Ramesh feels hurt, even more than if she had shouted, because her calm shows she has stopped counting on him.

grounding: It shows a teenager whose father keeps missing promised events, reading it as proof she is not a priority and stopping asking.

passage:
"Varun, get ready, Papa will take you for your driving practice at six," Mummy called.
"He won't."
"He promised this morning."
"He promised last Sunday. And the one before."
At six-thirty, the phone rang. Mummy answered. "Lalit, you promised him."
Varun heard his father's voice through the speaker. "Something came up at the shop. Tell him next week, pakka."
Mummy put the phone down. "Varun, beta—"
"It's fine."
"It's not fine."
"Mummy, it's fine. I'll ask Rohan's brother. He's teaching Rohan."
"You can still ask your Papa—"
"Why would I ask? He'll say yes and then not come."
Mummy sat down on the bed beside him. "Varun, I'm going to tell him how you feel, tonight."
Varun shrugged. "You can tell him. I've stopped hoping."

qa.q: What time did Mummy say Papa would take Varun for driving practice?
qa.a: At six.

qa.q: What was Varun feeling when he said "I've stopped hoping"?
qa.a: Varun felt deeply disappointed and resigned, protecting himself by no longer expecting his father to keep promises.

qa.q: How could Mummy support Varun now?
qa.a: She could stay with him, listen, and speak to Lalit that night about how the broken promises are affecting Varun.

qa.q: What would change if Lalit kept even one of these promises?
qa.a: Varun might start to believe his father's words again and feel he matters, instead of turning to Rohan's brother.

grounding: It shows a teenager whose father keeps breaking small promises, and how repeated letdowns teach him to stop hoping and stop asking.

passage:
My name is Hansa, and I stopped asking Papa for things when I was fourteen.
He had promised to take me to the planetarium for my birthday. I had wanted to go since I was small. The first time, he had an urgent meeting. The second time, he forgot. The third time, he said, "Next month for sure, my girl." Next month came and went, and he didn't mention it.
I remember sitting by the window with my star book on my lap, waiting for him to remember. He didn't.
After that, when he said, "I'll come to your sports day," I just said, "Okay." Inside, I didn't expect anything. It was easier than being disappointed.
Last month he asked, "Why don't you tell me anything anymore?" I didn't know how to explain that I had learned it, one little broken promise at a time.

qa.q: Where had Papa promised to take Hansa for her birthday?
qa.a: He had promised to take her to the planetarium.

qa.q: How did Hansa feel sitting by the window with the star book?
qa.a: Hansa felt hopeful at first and then deeply disappointed as Papa didn't remember.

qa.q: What could Papa do now that Hansa has stopped asking?
qa.a: He could admit the broken promises, apologise plainly, and keep one small promise, like the planetarium, to start rebuilding trust.

qa.q: How might Papa feel when he asks why Hansa doesn't tell him anything?
qa.a: Papa probably feels hurt and confused, not realising that his many small broken promises taught her to stop asking.

grounding: It shows a teenager whose father repeatedly broke small promises, teaching her to stop hoping and stop asking.
